questions.question: Why is Parquet faster for analytics queries than CSV?
options: It is text-based and human readable
It is column-oriented, so the engine can skip reading unnecessary columns
It is owned by a major cloud vendor
It always uses fewer rows
questions.explanation: Analytics queries typically need a few specific columns (e.g., AVG(price)), not every column in every row. Parquet's columnar layout lets the query engine skip columns it doesn't need, while CSV/JSON (row-oriented) must read full rows regardless.

questions.question: An API call to the BrightCart orders endpoint returns HTTP 429. What should the ingestion script do?
options: Immediately retry as fast as possible in a tight loop
Crash and alert an engineer
Wait using exponential backoff (with jitter) before retrying
Switch to a different API key and ignore the limit
questions.explanation: 429 means 'Too Many Requests' (rate limit exceeded). Production pipelines use exponential backoff with jitter -- waiting progressively longer between retries, with some randomness -- to avoid overwhelming the API and to avoid many clients retrying in lockstep ('thundering herd').

questions.question: In the BrightCart pagination exercise, the loop fetches pages until `next_page` is null. If the engineer forgets to update `current_page` inside the loop, what happens?
options: The loop fetches each page exactly once and stops correctly
The loop becomes infinite, repeatedly fetching the same page
The script raises a syntax error
The API automatically advances the page for you
questions.explanation: If `current_page` never changes, the while-loop condition (`current_page is not None`) stays true forever, and the same page is fetched repeatedly -- an infinite loop. This is why pagination loops must always reassign the loop variable from the response's `next_page` field.

questions.question: A nested JSON record for one BrightCart customer contains an `events` array with 3 events. After flattening, how many rows should that customer produce?
options: 1 row, with the array stored as a single JSON column
3 rows, one per event, all sharing the customer's other fields
0 rows, because arrays cannot be flattened
Exactly as many rows as there are total customers in the dataset
questions.explanation: Flattening (unnesting/exploding) a nested array produces one output row per array element, with the parent record's fields (like `user`) repeated on each row. A customer with 3 events becomes 3 rows.

questions.question: A BrightCart order record arrives missing the required `order_id` field. Per the schema-contract/validation pattern in this lesson, what is the best handling?
options: Silently drop the record with no trace
Crash the entire ingestion pipeline so no other records load
Route it to a quarantine table/dead-letter queue and continue processing the rest
Auto-generate a random order_id and load it as if nothing happened
questions.explanation: Quarantining invalid records preserves them for review/audit while letting the pipeline keep processing valid records. Silently dropping loses the audit trail; crashing the whole pipeline turns one bad record into a total outage; inventing data corrupts the warehouse.

questions.question: What is the main difference between polling an API on a schedule and using a webhook for ingestion?
options: Webhooks require no authentication at all
Polling pushes data to you; webhooks require you to ask for it
Webhooks push events to your endpoint as they happen; polling requires you to repeatedly ask the source if anything is new
There is no practical difference
questions.explanation: Polling means your pipeline calls the API on a schedule (e.g., every hour) to check for new data, adding latency. A webhook means the source system pushes an event to your endpoint the instant something happens (e.g., an order ships), reducing latency but requiring you to run a reliable always-on receiver.

questions.question: Why is an incremental extraction 'watermark' useful for nightly BrightCart order loads?
options: It encrypts the data in transit
It lets the pipeline only request records updated since the last successful run, instead of re-pulling the full history
It compresses the JSON payload automatically
It is required by every REST API regardless of use case
questions.explanation: A watermark (the last successfully ingested timestamp/ID) lets you query for only new/changed records (`updated_since=watermark`). Without it, every run would have to re-extract the entire dataset, which is slow and costly at scale.

questions.question: Storing 100 GB of BrightCart order_items as Snappy-compressed Parquet instead of raw CSV typically results in roughly what storage reduction?
options: No meaningful reduction -- formats use about the same space
About 95% smaller (e.g., 100 GB down to roughly 5 GB)
Exactly 50% smaller, always
It becomes larger because Parquet stores schema metadata
questions.explanation: Columnar dictionary/run-length encoding (e.g., a repeated 'web' channel value) plus Snappy compression typically shrinks data by roughly 10x from columnar encoding and another ~2x from compression -- around a 95% total reduction versus raw CSV, which directly reduces cloud storage cost.
